method: Each rung is sized from the previous one: the height is multiplied by the chosen step ratio (three quarters, two thirds or one half) and rounded to the nearest even pixel, and the width follows the top frame's aspect ratio, also rounded to even pixels, because encoders and hardware scalers expect even dimensions. The video bitrate is the target bits per pixel per frame multiplied by width x height x frame rate, rounded to a whole kilobit per second, and the rung's audio bitrate is added to give the total muxed bitrate. Storage per minute is total bitrate x 60 / 8 in decimal megabytes, storage per hour is total bitrate x 3600 / 8 in decimal gigabytes, and peak egress is the viewer count times the top rung's total bitrate. The ladder stops before a rung would fall below 64 pixels in either direction or repeat the previous height, so a small top frame can produce fewer rungs than requested; that case is reported rather than invented. The default 1920x1080, 30 fps, 0.08 bits per pixel ladder with 128 kbps audio gives 1920x1080 at 4,977 kbps video and 5,105 kbps total, then 1280x720 at 2,212 and 2,340 kbps, 854x480 at 984 and 1,112 kbps, and 568x320 at 436 and 564 kbps: 9,121 kbps across the ladder, 4.10 GB for an hour of every rung, and 510.50 Mbps of peak egress for 100 viewers on the top rung. Bits per pixel is only a planning heuristic; codec, preset, scene complexity, keyframe density and per-title tuning all change the real figure, and audio is assumed to be the same on every rung. Values are whole numbers of pixels, frames per second, kilobits per second and viewers, with bits per pixel limited to three decimal places between 0.005 and 1, and text, negatives, exponent notation and out-of-range values are refused with the field named. The page calculates locally and stores, uploads and transmits nothing.

sources.title: Adaptive bitrate streaming: a rendition ladder pairs resolutions with bitrates so a player can pick the rung that fits the measured bandwidth.
Bits per pixel per frame, bitrate divided by width x height x frame rate, is a common heuristic for comparing encoder settings across resolutions.
